name: Adobe brick building on the north coast of Peru
summary: Builders at Los Morteros on Peru’s north coast used cut natural clay bricks as the main material in a monumental building.
description: At Los Morteros in the lower Chao Valley, builders laid rectangular clay bricks in mud mortar above a stone foundation. Preserved laminations and comparison with modern flood-laid clay led excavators to infer that builders cut the bricks from a natural deposit. Later Peruvian adobe was typically made from mixtures of clay, temper and water.

impact.note: The paper says adobe defined the major building traditions of the Andes for thousands of years, from Moche pyramids and Chan Chan to rural houses today, which is many societies of one civilisation over generations (reach 2); it gave coastal builders a new material around which building was later reorganised (depth 2); its known successors are improvements of the brick itself, tempered, conical and mould-made (generativity 1).

date.label: 5,500 to 5,100 cal BP (c. 3550 to 3150 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: In Phase II-2 at Los Morteros, builders erected brick walls on stone and mortar foundations. Excavators place room use at 5,500–5,100 cal BP, using stratigraphy and dated offerings associated with closure.

evidence.locator: The Adobes of Los Morteros, Fig. 1 and Table 1
evidence.supports: Documents the walls and their earlier and closing contexts. Table 1 records no radiocarbon sample directly dating the Phase II-2 architecture.

evidence.locator: Results, Structure and Grain Size of Adobe Bricks, Figs. 2–4
evidence.supports: Lamination, fine sediment and comparison with samples from a modern flood deposit support cutting blocks from naturally laid clay.

events.caveats: The dated offerings and earlier deposits constrain the building chronology. The walls were not directly dated, and the exact clay source remains open.

date.label: from the Initial Period, around 3,600 cal BP (c. 1650 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Adobes of later periods, starting in the Initial Period around 3,600 cal BP (about 1650 BCE), were normally made by mixing clay and water with other materials.

evidence.supports: Available information shows that adobes made in later periods (starting in the Initial Period around 3,600 cal y B.P. and continuing to present) were normally produced using a combination of clay, water, and other elements

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The site coordinates are the ones printed in the Quaternary Research abstract (8 deg 39' 54" S, 78 deg 42' 00" W); no event quotes that paper.
The age of the undated lower Component I at Los Morteros is not given, so the earliest construction may be older than 5,500 cal BP.

The paper says widespread use of adobe is not recorded until the Initial Period and that adobe became the primary coastal building material only in the Early Intermediate Period; it gives no calendar date for the latter in the passages read.
Whether the 'at least two hand-formed dried-mud bricks' from Nanchoc (Las Pircas Phase, about 9,800 to 7,800 cal BP) count as earlier adobe is not settled by the paper.
Mesoamerican adobe is probably a separate origin and needs its own record.

unresolved.about: Within-site development from earlier clay surfaces
unresolved.note: Phase II-1 includes clay surfaces and hearths below the adobe building. Whether the occupants shared material sources or passed on methods from that occupation to the wall builders remains unknown.

evidence.locator: The Adobes of Los Morteros and Table 1
evidence.supports: The earlier clay surfaces and the Phase II-2 brick construction are stratigraphically distinct.

research.note: The paper calls Los Morteros the earliest adobe monumental building in the Americas and describes adobe as invented there from local flood-laid clay; at about 3550 to 3150 BCE no knowledge of Old World mud brick could have reached Peru, so contact is excluded. Two or three older hand-formed mud blocks reported from Nanchoc, in the same region, leave open where on the north coast the idea began.
